analyses.title: On the difference between updating a knowledge base and revising it
analyses.research_question: How should knowledge-base update for a changing world be distinguished from revision prompted by new information about a static world, and what does that distinction imply for rationality postulates governing belief change?
analyses.methodology: The paper takes a conceptual and formal knowledge-representation approach, representing a knowledge base as a logical theory and newly acquired information as a sentence to be incorporated. It contrasts two classes of knowledge-base modification through examples such as database changes and changes caused by robot actions. The analysis evaluates the applicability of AGM-style rationality postulates to these different kinds of change.

key_findings.finding: Knowledge-base update and revision are fundamentally different operations: update concerns a world that has changed, whereas revision concerns new information about a world treated as static.
A single set of rationality postulates is not adequate for every knowledge-base modification application.
The AGM postulates developed for belief revision require substantial modification when the intended operation is update.
Ordinary database changes and state changes caused by a robot's actions are examples of update because they alter the represented world rather than merely correcting beliefs about an unchanged world.

limitations: Only the publisher's summary and introductory extract were accessible in this review, so the paper's complete formal postulates, proofs, and representation results could not be independently inspected.
The accessible discussion is framed around logical, particularly propositional, representations of knowledge bases rather than empirical operational communication data.
No empirical evaluation, software artifact, dataset, or quantitative metric is described in the accessible extract.
raw_claims: Knowledge-base change can correspond either to a change in the represented world or to new information about an unchanged world.
Update is the operation intended to bring a knowledge base into line with a changing world.
Revision is intended for incorporating new information about a world assumed to remain static.
The same rationality requirements need not be appropriate for all forms of knowledge-base change.
AGM-style revision requirements are not directly adequate as a theory of update.
Database modifications that change a fact in the modeled domain are paradigmatic update cases.
Changes caused by an acting robot also motivate an update semantics rather than ordinary belief revision.

analyses.title: Towards Generative Event Factuality Prediction
analyses.research_question: Can an end-to-end generative model predict source-relative event factuality, including factuality holders, target events, and factuality values, and can output design and multi-task learning improve that prediction?
analyses.methodology: The authors construct usable projections of FactBank for source-and-target factuality and author-only factuality and formulate prediction as text generation of structured factuality tuples or triplets. They fine-tune Flan-T5-base and compare alternative output representations, text normalization, and multi-task mixtures involving FactBank and other factuality or cognitive-state corpora. Source-and-target performance is evaluated primarily with exact-match triplet F1 plus source and target F1 measures, while author-only experiments use exact-match and macro-F1 evaluations. Experimental results are averaged across three fixed random seeds with reported standard deviations.

key_findings.finding: Event factuality is modeled as the factuality presentation or judgment attributed to an author or other source, rather than as direct determination of objective real-world truth.
Text normalization increased the source-and-target FactBank baseline exact-match triplet F1 from 0.472 to 0.512, with much of the improvement attributed to morphology and orthography corrections.
key_findings.section: 6.2 Results: Baseline and Target Output Restructuring

key_findings.finding: Multi-task learning with the author-only FactBank projection substantially improved source-and-target prediction, with the FBST plus FBAO* configuration reaching an exact-match triplet F1 of 0.684 compared with 0.535 for the reported Table 4 baseline.
For author-only FactBank prediction, the multi-task FBAO* plus FBST configuration achieved exact-match F1 of 0.897, compared with 0.866 for the basic FBAO configuration.
The structure of generated output materially affects results; in the author-only exact-match evaluation, inline annotation generation performed worse than tuple or triplet generation.

Source identification was consistently easier than target identification in the source-and-target baseline experiments, showing that correctly pairing a factuality holder with its target event remains difficult.
key_findings.section: 6.2 Results: Baseline and Target Output Restructuring

limitations: The machine-learning experiments do not represent the complete hierarchy of nested factuality sources; they focus on the last nested source.
All reported experiments use Flan-T5-base, so conclusions about the generative formulation are not demonstrated across substantially different model families.
The authors characterize the FactBank source-and-target projection and results as preliminary.
Potential biases introduced or amplified during language-model fine-tuning were not experimentally analyzed.
raw_claims: The task represents factuality as a source's presentation of whether an event is factual rather than as an objective truth label.
The source-and-target task generates a source, target event, and factuality label together.
FactBank contains nested sources whose factuality judgments can differ from the author's judgment.
The authors created a database representation of FactBank and made the FactBank database available through a public GitHub repository.
All reported model experiments use Flan-T5-base.
Normalization improved the basic source-and-target exact-match triplet score.
The authors report that source spans are generally easier to generate correctly than target spans.
Multi-task learning with author-only FactBank data produced the strongest reported source-and-target triplet result.
Author-only factuality prediction benefited from combining its training data with source-and-target FactBank data.
Inline output annotation was less effective than structured tuple generation under the author-only exact-match evaluation.
The experiments retain only the final nested source instead of reconstructing the complete chain of embedded sources.

analyses.title: An Empirical Characterization of Event Sourced Systems and Their Schema Evolution - Lessons from Industry
analyses.research_question: How are event-sourced systems used and defined in industry, how do practitioners evolve their event data structures, and what recurring engineering challenges arise?
analyses.methodology: The study applies constructivist grounded theory to industrial event sourcing. The authors conducted 22 interviews involving 25 engineers and discuss 19 event-sourced systems, recruiting participants through practitioner communities, direct invitations, and interview snowballing. Interview material was iteratively coded into concepts and categories, while related literature and the authors' earlier event-sourcing research were incorporated during the grounded-theory process. The resulting characterization combines practitioners' reported motivations, system properties, challenges, and schema-evolution practices.

key_findings.finding: Practitioners reported five major challenges: evolving event systems, a steep learning curve, insufficient technology support, rebuilding projections, and data privacy.
key_findings.section: 6 Challenges Faced in Applying Event Sourcing

key_findings.finding: The study identifies five event-schema evolution techniques used in practice: versioned events, weak schema, upcasting, in-place transformation, and copy-and-transform.
key_findings.section: 7 Schema Evolution in Event Sourced Systems

key_findings.finding: No single schema-evolution technique is appropriate in every context; versioned events and weak schema are presented as comparatively simple starting points, upcasting as a way to retain event-store immutability, and copy-and-transform as an option when performance or maintainability motivates a more expensive transformation.
key_findings.section: 7 Schema Evolution in Event Sourced Systems

key_findings.finding: Copy-and-transform preserves the original source events while creating new transformed event streams, allowing historical source events to remain immutable.
key_findings.section: 7 Schema Evolution in Event Sourced Systems

key_findings.finding: Immutability was not universal in the 19 studied systems: eight never changed events, three permitted controlled cut-off changes backed by retained backups, and eight allowed event changes without indefinitely retained backups; the last group therefore did not preserve a complete audit trail.

Retention of state changes was an important audit rationale for adopting event sourcing, while other reported rationales included architectural flexibility, handling business complexity, and following an industry trend.

limitations: The authors explicitly state that the number of interviews does not support broad statistical generalization or hard recommendations.
Participants volunteered after recruitment through event-sourcing communities and referrals, creating possible self-selection bias.
The study did not reach grounded-theory saturation, so relevant concepts or practices may have been missed.
Sixteen of the 25 engineers had three years or less of event-sourcing experience.
Many studied systems were closed-source commercial systems, limiting validation through source code or documentation.
The encountered systems were concentrated in enterprise applications; the study did not encounter event-sourced IoT or other stream-processing systems.
raw_claims: The empirical study covers 19 event-sourced systems through interviews with 25 engineers.
The authors conducted 22 distinct interviews because several interviews included two engineers working on the same system.
Event-system evolution was one of the central engineering difficulties reported by practitioners.
The study identifies versioned events, weak schema, upcasting, in-place transformation, and copy-and-transform as schema-evolution techniques.
Practitioners frequently combine more than one evolution technique rather than selecting one universal strategy.
Copy-and-transform creates transformed streams without modifying the source events.
Upcasting is presented as an evolution mechanism that retains event-store immutability.
Some production event-sourced systems permit modification of stored events and therefore do not maintain a complete immutable audit trail.
Preserving historical state changes is one reason practitioners adopt event sourcing.
The sample was recruited pragmatically from practitioner communities and through snowball referrals.
The authors do not claim that grounded-theory saturation was achieved.
The qualitative sample is not sufficient to infer that the most commonly observed technique is universally preferable.

analyses.title: Agreement, Disputes and Commitments in Dialogue
analyses.research_question: How can dialogue semantics represent agreement, disagreement, correction, and changing commitments in a logically consistent way while accounting for implicit agreement and preservation of undisputed prior content?
analyses.methodology: The paper develops a formal semantic theory based on Segmented Discourse Representation Theory, extending dialogue logical forms so that each participant has a distinct representation of public commitments. It defines agreement through shared entailments and introduces dynamic update and persistence principles governing acceptance, correction, and correction of corrections. The formal machinery includes Dialogue SDRSs, dynamic semantic interpretation, rhetorical relations, and glue-logic axioms for undenied commitments. The theory is demonstrated on constructed and naturally occurring dialogue examples rather than evaluated through a quantitative benchmark.

key_findings.finding: Agreement can be defined as shared entailments of the dialogue participants' public commitments, including commitments introduced by rhetorical relations, which permits logically explicit treatment of implicit agreement.

Keeping each participant's commitments in a separate information structure allows participants to hold mutually inconsistent positions while the dialogue representation itself remains interpretable rather than collapsing into inconsistency.
When a speaker accepts a correction, the update should remove commitments that are disavowed while preserving parts of earlier contributions that were not denied.
A correction can target a rhetorical relation rather than all of the underlying propositional content, so disagreement does not imply that every proposition in the corrected contribution is rejected.

When a correction is itself corrected, the Denying Corrections principle normally restores the relevant earlier, undenied commitment structure and makes prior material available again, providing a formal account of reopening a previously disputed commitment.
The persistence axioms follow a general strategy of preserving as much prior commitment as possible while remaining consistent with the illocutionary effect of the participant's current utterance.

limitations: The authors describe the work as initial steps toward a broader dynamic theory of grounding.
The paper does not provide a detailed account of how questions and imperatives change commitments, agreement, or disputes.
Connections from public commitments to private attitudes such as beliefs, preferences, and intentions are left for future work.
Pragmatic phenomena such as accusation and assignment of blame are not fully modeled.
The formal theory is illustrated with dialogue examples but is not subjected to corpus-scale quantitative evaluation.
raw_claims: Dialogue interpretation should distinguish the public commitments of individual participants.
Agreement is modeled through entailments shared by the participants' public commitment states.
Rhetorical relations contribute to commitments and therefore affect what counts as implicit agreement.
Two participants can maintain mutually inconsistent commitments without making each participant's own information state inconsistent.
A dispute can reject a rhetorical connection without rejecting every proposition associated with the earlier contribution.
Updates after a dispute must determine which earlier commitments persist and which are dropped.
A participant who accepts a correction normally retains earlier content that the correction did not deny.
The persistence mechanism is sensitive to the type and scope of the current speech act.
A correction of another correction can make commitments from before the dispute relevant and available again.
The formal persistence rules seek to retain prior commitments whenever doing so is consistent with the current utterance.
Questions and imperatives are not analyzed in the same detail as assertions, acceptances, and corrections.

analyses.title: Resolution of time concepts in temporal databases
analyses.research_question: Which temporal dimensions and validity concepts are necessary to preserve database history precisely and losslessly when information may be entered retroactively, proactively, corrected, or recorded after a delay?
analyses.methodology: The paper takes a formal temporal-database approach, defining temporal validity and extending it to interpretation-based validity in order to distinguish previously conflated notions of time. It analyzes what temporal dimensions are required to preserve multiple past states under different kinds of update. The authors then characterize object history along valid time and sketch how such history can be implemented in the relational data model.

key_findings.finding: Three distinct temporal concepts are required for the paper's account of precise and lossless preservation of temporal database information.
Valid time and transaction time alone cannot correctly represent retroactive and proactive updates; event time is additionally required.

The combination of event time, valid time, and transaction time is presented as adequate for preserving past states generated by retroactive updates, proactive updates, error corrections, and delayed updates.
Temporal validity and interpretation-based validity are introduced to clarify the semantics of different time concepts and to define an object's evolution along the valid-time dimension.
The paper sketches a relational-data-model implementation for retaining object history rather than treating the formal distinctions only as abstract semantics.

limitations: Only the abstract was accessible from the primary publication source during this review, so the formal definitions, proofs, examples, and implementation details could not be independently inspected.
The accessible evidence establishes a formal adequacy argument rather than an empirical performance evaluation.
The implementation is described in the abstract as a sketch, so no claim about production-scale feasibility or performance can be established from the accessible text.
No released software, experimental dataset, or quantitative evaluation metric is identified in the accessible abstract.
raw_claims: The paper distinguishes three temporal concepts for lossless temporal information preservation.
Temporal validity is formally distinguished from an extended interpretation-based notion of validity.
Preserving multiple historical database states motivates the need to separate different temporal dimensions.
Valid time and transaction time are insufficient by themselves for retroactive and proactive updates.
Event time provides information needed to model those update cases correctly.
Event, valid, and transaction times together are presented as sufficient for preserving histories involving retroactive and proactive updates.
The same three-dimensional treatment covers histories affected by error correction and delayed recording.
Object history can be characterized along valid time using the proposed validity semantics.
The paper includes a sketch of how retained history can be represented in a relational data model.
